video.title: Forget Snack Machines. This One Refills Itself

summary: Chris Koerner interviews CJ, a Fort Worth operator of four outdoor ice and water vending machines (Everest, Cooler Ice, Twice the Ice, and a large Ice House America-style unit) with no employees beyond one part-time maintenance tech. CJ explains how he got in via his pool-service business's ice spend, why buying distressed existing machines and locations beats building from scratch, how revenue-share vs flat-rent leases work, and the claimed ~90% gross margins. He also covers sale multiples of 2-3x annual profit, avoiding financing, and low-cost entry from $500-$1,000 for a used small machine. Key takeaway: location and buying out stressed single-machine owners are the main levers, but the business needs physical servicing.

speakers.name: CJ
speakers.description: Fort Worth ice/water vending operator and real estate investor (Lovest Realty DFW); ex-owner of DFW Pool Services

ideas.name: Outdoor ice and water vending machine network
ideas.one_liner: Own several self-serve ice and water vending machines on leased lots, bought used from distressed owners, serviced by one part-time tech.
ideas.business_model: Per-sale coin/cash/card vending of bagged ice and water; revenue share or flat lease with landlord.
ideas.customer: Tradespeople (pool, yard, electrical crews), contractors, boaters/weekenders, and general public needing cheap ice and water.
ideas.problem: Gas stations and grocers charge high prices for ice (about $4 for 7 lb at CVS/Walgreens); trades buy ice daily.
ideas.offer: 10 lb ice for $2 and 20 lb for $3.50, plus purified water, available 24/7 from street-front machines.

acquisition_channels.details: Drive-by traffic at high-count locations (30-50k cars/day); parking and trailer access matter. Existing machines bring established clientele (this one since ~2008).
Repeat daily trade customers (pool, yard, electrical crews) who find it cheaper than the gas station.
Sourcing machines and deals (not customers) by networking with other owners on Facebook and calling numbers printed on machines.

ideas.delivery: Machines make and dispense ice automatically. Operator or a roughly $600-$1,000/month tech visits to clear jams, clean, fix parts, collect coins and cash, and test. Remote reset and free-dispense via phone app.
unit_economics_claims: Bag costs 7-10 cents; ice/water ~10-15 cents; ~90% margin per bag
Best location 2-3k/month typical, up to 4-5k busy season; 30% revenue share
Four locations hoped to total 15-20k/month revenue, ~5k/month cost
Payback of 100% of money in 1-3 years
tools: Machine app for remote control and counters
ideas.startup_cost: $500-$1,000 for a used small machine, up to ~$2,500; large Ice House style units $150k-$500k; delivery of machines a couple hundred dollars; may need $10-30k of repair work.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Buying an existing location: immediate (first Saturday $1,000-1,500). Building new: 60-90 days best case, possibly 6-9 months due to permitting.

acquisition.how: Customers are walk-up traffic driven by location; sourcing locations and deals is manual networking, calling and driving around. Software could help find sites but not close them.

onboarding.how: No customer onboarding; the machines are self-serve.

delivery.how: Physical servicing, cleaning, jam clearing, coin and cash collection and repairs need a human on site; remote resets cover only software faults.

billing.how: Coin, cash and card are collected at the machine; the only manual steps are coin and cash collection and paying the landlord.

support.how: Jams and faults are reported by phone call or text and can often be reset remotely via the app; physical faults need a tech.

uk_applicability.notes: The model depends on US ice-vending culture, hot Texas climate, car-centric lots and cheap parking; UK demand for bagged ice is lower and seasonal, and councils may require planning or permits. Cheap-ice price gaps against UK supermarkets are likely smaller.

risks: Break-ins and vandalism (one location down for months after being drilled through)
Financed owners get squeezed by slow months
Used machines may need $10-30k of repair
City permitting and code delays for new builds
Location dependence; big machines are hard to move

ideas.name: Buy distressed existing ice machines and locations
ideas.one_liner: Acquire stressed single-machine owners' ice stations cheaply rather than building from scratch.
ideas.business_model: Buy machines/locations at a discount, repair, and operate or resell.
ideas.customer: Older or overwhelmed single-machine owners looking to exit.
ideas.problem: Single-machine owners are stressed by breakdowns and want out; new builds face permits and unknown locations.
ideas.offer: Take over a machine with established clientele, often for a fraction of its value; a friend got one for $500 worth about 10-15k.

pricing.model: Negotiated purchase; typical multiple 2-3x annual profit
pricing.notes: One seller asking $400-500k for a ~15k/month location (about 3.25x).

acquisition_channels.details: Network with local owners on Facebook; call or text numbers printed on machines.
Manufacturers (Everest, Cooler Ice, Twice the Ice) help find locations or sales.

ideas.delivery: Operator takes over the machine and fixes it.
unit_economics_claims: Machine bought for $500 worth 10-15k, being resold for 15-20k
ideas.startup_cost: Low as $500-$1,000; potentially $10-30k of repair work.

acquisition.how: Deal sourcing relies on calling and relationships; cold texting individuals is restricted in the UK under PECR.

support.how: Remote app resets with human on-site backup.

uk_applicability.notes: Same constraints as the base ice business; UK market for ice machines is much smaller.

tactics.name: Find and buy from stressed single-machine owners
steps: Drive around looking for machines in your area
Call or text the owner numbers printed on the machine
Look for owners with a single machine who are exhausted by breakdowns
Offer to take it over; consider sellers who have let machines go
Network with owners on Facebook and ask how they started

quote.text: if you could go to the machines in your area and just call the owners and finally catch one

tactics.name: Pick locations by traffic and access
steps: Check traffic counts on a .gov site
Use revenue share at very busy sites to share downside

tactics.name: Hire one roaming tech
steps: Visit all machines to clear jams and clean
Operator remotely resets and dispenses free water from the app

lessons.lesson: Turn a cost centre you know well into a business; the operator started because his pool company spent thousands a month on ice.

quote.text: how do we turn this cost center into a profit center?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Buying a running asset from a tired owner usually beats building from scratch on price, speed and risk.

quote.text: they're going to pay a ton more if they started from scratch
quote.speaker: CJ

lessons.lesson: Revenue-share leases align landlord incentives and share downside during outages, at the cost of a lower margin.
Start small with one unit and grow from cash flow rather than debt.

quote.text: I recommend starting small getting one and building it up
quote.speaker: CJ

lessons.lesson: Seasonality matters; winter revenue can fall to a tenth of peak.
Physical servicing is the bottleneck for scaling unattended assets; a single roaming tech lets one owner handle several machines.
Unglamorous niches with fragmented, ageing local owners offer roll-up opportunities.

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand operator with several specific figures, but numbers are rough and partly hopeful (new location projections, an unknown fraction of total revenue). The profit figures are not reconciled and the host leads with hype.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Guest promotes his real estate team and YouTube channel (Lovest Realty DFW); host asks for subscribes.
